sections.h: The Two Ways in the Didache
sections.b: The Didache opens: "There are two ways, one of life and one of death, and there is a great difference between the two ways" (Didache 1:1). The way of life is love of God and neighbor and the negative Golden Rule (1:2), spelled out in sayings like the Sermon on the Mount (1:3-6), a widened list of the commandments (2:2-7), the "my child" sayings that trace great sins to small ones (3:1-6), and duties to teachers, the poor, children and slaves (4:1-14). The way of death is a list of sins and sinners (5:1-2). The same teaching, under light and darkness, closes the Epistle of Barnabas (Barnabas 18-20). Lake thought most scholars saw a common source behind both, which "many think" was a Jewish document for teaching converts. In the Didache the Two Ways is taught before baptism: "First say all these things, then baptize" (Didache 7:1).
sections.refs: Didache 1:1-6:3; Didache 7:1; Barnabas 18:1-20:2; Deuteronomy 30:15-19; Jeremiah 21:8; Matthew 7:13-14

common: Lake: the Two Ways is "a statement of the principles of Christian conduct, which is to be taught to catechumens before their baptism."
uncommon: R. A. Kraft held that the Two Ways was "originally Jewish" and that the Gospel sayings of Didache 1:3b-2:1 are "a Christian contribution that may have been added by the Didachist himself."

sections.h: The thanksgiving prayers of the Didache
sections.b: Didache 9-10 gives a set of Christian meal prayers: thanks over the cup ("for the holy vine of your servant David"), then over the broken bread ("for the life and knowledge"), a prayer that the church be gathered like grain into one loaf, and after the meal a longer thanksgiving that ends "Marana tha! Amen." Only the baptized may eat and drink (9:5). The prayers do not mention Jesus' body and blood or his death, the cup comes before the bread, and the meal is a full one ("after you have eaten your fill," 10:1). Kraft says the prayers "at first glance" look like a Eucharist liturgy, that "many commentators" (among them G. Dix) took them as a love feast, and himself placed them at a yearly service for the newly baptized. Chapter 14 adds the Sunday gathering: "break bread and give thanks," confess first, be reconciled, so that "your sacrifice" is pure, with Malachi 1:11 as proof.
sections.refs: Didache 9:1-10:7; Didache 14:1-3; 1 Corinthians 10:16-17; 1 Corinthians 11:20-26; Luke 22:17-20; Acts 2:42-46

common: Kraft: "At first glance" the prayers of Didache 9-10 "seem to represent a 'Eucharist' liturgy."
uncommon: G. Dix (1945), as Kraft reports, read Didache 9-10 as a love feast, a fellowship meal patterned on Jewish meals.

sections.b: Didache 7 says how to baptize. After the Two Ways has been taught, the candidate is baptized "into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19's words), preferably "in living water," running water from a spring or stream; if there is none, in other water, cold or warm; and if there is not enough for that, by pouring water three times on the head, which Kraft calls "probably the earliest reference to that practice in Christianity." The one who baptizes, the one being baptized and others fast beforehand, the candidate one or two days. Only the baptized share the thanksgiving meal (9:5). The site's cards at Acts 8 (immersion) and Matthew 28 (the words) set out how churches use these rules today.

sections.h: The Lord's Prayer in the Didache
sections.b: Didache 8:2 gives the Lord's Prayer "as the Lord commanded in his good news," in a form very close to Matthew's, and 8:3 says to pray it three times a day. The differences are small: "heaven" in the singular, "the debt" for "the debts," "we forgive" for "we have forgiven," and a closing line of praise, "For yours is the power and the glory forever," without "kingdom" or "Amen." Kraft notes that this doxology "seems to have been known in Egypt (see the Coptic versions of Matt. 6:13) and Syria"; the oldest manuscripts of Matthew have none (see the variant at Matthew 6:13). The prayer is set against praying "like the hypocrites" (8:2), as in Matthew 6:5-9.

The Didache asks for fasting before baptism by the one baptizing, the candidate and others (7:4), and gives the church its own weekly fast days: "Your fasts must not be with the hypocrites. For they fast on the second day of the week and the fifth. But you are to fast on the fourth day and on Preparation Day" (8:1), Wednesday and Friday instead of Monday and Thursday. Jesus' Pharisee fasts "Twice a week" (Luke 18:12), without naming the days; the Mishnah starts a series of public fasts for rain on "a Monday, Thursday, and the following Monday" (Mishnah Taanit 2:9). Kraft takes the Didache's Monday and Thursday as the "(Pharisaic) Jewish fasts" and notes that the Wednesday and Friday fasts "were widely observed in early Christianity." The church fasts twice a week, but by design on other days. 1:3 adds a fast "for the people who persecute you."

sections.b: The Didache shows prophets as a living part of church life in the period behind the book (its date is argued). They travel and may settle (13:1); they give thanks at the meal in their own words (10:7); they receive the firstfruits, "for they are your high priests" (13:3). A prophet speaking in the Spirit is not to be tested or judged, for that "sin will not be forgiven" (11:7), but "not everyone who speaks in the Spirit is a prophet": he must have "the Lord's ways" (11:8). A prophet who orders a meal and eats it, does not practice what he teaches, or asks money for himself is false (11:9-12). Overseers and deacons "too perform for you the service of the prophets and teachers" (15:1).
sections.refs: Didache 10:7; Didache 11:7-12; Didache 13:1-7; Didache 15:1-2; 1 Corinthians 14:29-32; 1 John 4:1; Matthew 7:15-20

sections.h: "The Lord's day of the Lord" in the Didache
sections.b: Didache 14:1 sets the gathering on the Lord's day, which Kraft takes as "probably" the regular Sunday meeting (C. W. Dugmore argued for Easter only): "On the Lord's day of the Lord, when you have gathered, break bread and give thanks." The Greek kyriakē, "the Lord's (day)," is the word of Revelation 1:10. The Didache does not mention the Sabbath or say that Sunday replaces it; it simply sets the gathering on the Lord's day, as Acts 20:7 and 1 Corinthians 16:2 speak of the first day of the week. The Apostolic Constitutions later calls it "the day of the resurrection of the Lord, that is, the Lord's day" (book 7, chapter 30). The site's cards at Revelation 1 and Exodus 20 give the churches' views on Sunday and the Sabbath.

sections.h: "Let your alms sweat in your hands" (Didache 1:6)
sections.b: Didache 1:6 introduces a saying with "it has also been said": "Let your alms sweat in your hands until you know who you are giving to." No book of the Bible has these words. It warns against careless giving and seems to qualify the command just before it, "Keep giving to anyone who asks you" (1:5, from Luke 6:30). Sirach has a similar thought: "If you do a kindness, know who you are doing it for" (Sirach 12:1). The Didache does not say whether the saying is the Lord's.

The Didache shares much with Matthew: the Lord's Prayer in Matthew's form (8:2), the threefold name for baptism (7:1; Matthew 28:19), "Do not give what is holy to the dogs" (9:5; Matthew 7:6), "has earned his food" (13:1; Matthew 10:10), and the end-time sayings of Matthew 24 in chapter 16. In 1:3-5 it mixes Matthew's and Luke's forms of the sermon sayings and adds words neither has. It speaks of "the good news" as something the church "has" (15:3-4). Whether it used written Gospels, the oral teaching behind them, or a sayings source like the one scholars call Q is argued; Kraft, following H. Koester, thinks it more likely that the Didache used sayings material that kept circulating after the Gospels were written. Its mixed and loose forms are evidence each view must explain.

sections.b: "You must not murder a child by abortion, and you must not kill one that has been born" (Didache 2:2) names abortion and the killing of newborns; Kraft notes the first line means abortion, "apparently before birth since infanticide is next mentioned." The way of death lists "murderers of children and destroyers of what God has formed" (5:2). The Epistle of Barnabas has the same commandment (Barnabas 19:5).

The title claims the book as "The teaching of the Lord through the twelve apostles" (Didache 1:0), but in chapter 11 "apostles" are traveling preachers. Lake: the word "does not mean a member of 'the Twelve,' but is merely an inspired teacher who is engaged in preaching, especially to those as yet unconverted." Such an apostle is welcomed "as the Lord," stays one day, or two if needed, takes only bread for the road, and if he asks for money "is a false prophet" (11:4-6).

Didache 15:1-2 tells each church to "choose for yourselves overseers and deacons who are worthy of the Lord": several overseers, chosen by the congregation (the verb first meant voting by a show of hands), with no single head named. They "too perform for you the service of the prophets and teachers," and the church must not "look down on them." The Didache does not use "elder." The arrangement is like Philippians 1:1, "with overseers and deacons."

Deacons are chosen with the overseers, "men who are gentle, free from the love of money, truthful and tested" (Didache 15:1), qualities that echo 1 Timothy 3:3 and 3:8-10. The Didache gives them no separate duties; with the overseers they "perform for you the service of the prophets and teachers."

The Didache gives a church practical tests for those who come claiming to teach or prophesy. The teaching must not "do away with" what has been taught (11:1-2). An apostle who stays three days or asks for money is a false prophet (11:5-6); so is a prophet who does not have "the Lord's ways," eats a meal he orders, does not practice what he teaches, or asks money for himself (11:8-12). A traveler who will not work is "a Christ-peddler" (12:5). In the last days "the false prophets and the corrupters will multiply" (16:3).

sections.b: Didache 16:4: as lawlessness grows, "the world-deceiver will appear as a son of God. He will do signs and wonders, and the earth will be handed over into his hands." The figure matches the lawless one of 2 Thessalonians 2:9 and the beast of Revelation 13, but the Didache's word, kosmoplanēs, is its own.

sections.h: The last days in the Didache
sections.b: The Didache ends with a warning drawn from Matthew 24: stay awake and be ready (16:1); come together often (16:2); in the last days false prophets multiply, sheep turn into wolves, love into hate (16:3); the world-deceiver appears (16:4); humankind comes into "the fire of testing" (16:5); then three "signs of the truth" (16:6) and the Lord comes "on the clouds of the sky" (16:8). The one complete Greek manuscript stops there; the Georgian version goes on to the judgment (Kraft).

The third sign of the end is "a resurrection of the dead," "But not of all the dead," only of the saints who come with the Lord, citing Zechariah 14:5 in its Greek form (Didache 16:6-7). Like 1 Thessalonians 4:16 and Revelation 20:5-6, the Didache places the rising of believers at the Lord's coming; it does not say what happens to the rest.

The thanksgiving after the meal ends: "Let grace come, and let this world pass away. Hosanna to the God of David! Whoever is holy, let him come. Whoever is not, let him repent. Marana tha! Amen" (Didache 10:6). Lake divides the Aramaic as maran atha; the site reads marana tha, "Our Lord, come!", as at 1 Corinthians 16:22.

The Didache asks for open-handed giving ("Keep giving to anyone who asks you," 1:5), warns those who take without need, and also says "Let your alms sweat in your hands until you know who you are giving to" (1:6). Giving is "ransom for your sins" (4:6), as in Daniel 4:27 and Tobit 12:9; one must not hesitate or grumble (4:7) or hold out the hand to take and pull it back from giving (4:5; Sirach 4:31). Prayers and alms are to be done "in the way you have it in our Lord's good news" (15:4).

sections.h: Welcome and its limits in the Didache
sections.b: "Everyone who comes in the Lord's name is to be welcomed" (Didache 12:1). The Didache then sets limits: a traveler may stay two or three days; one who settles must work; one with no trade is to be helped to work, not kept idle (12:2-4). Apostles stay one day or two (11:5).

A Christian who settles in a new church and has a trade "is to work and eat"; if he has none, the church is to plan "so that no Christian will live idle among you"; one who refuses is "a Christ-peddler" (Didache 12:3-5). Prophets and teachers who settle have "earned his food," like the worker of Matthew 10:10 (13:1-2).

sections.h: Parents, slaves and masters in the Didache
sections.b: The Two Ways includes a short household code: parents must not neglect their children but teach them "to fear God" from their youth; masters must not give orders "in bitterness" to slaves "who hope in the same God"; slaves are to submit to masters "as to a figure of God, with modesty and fear" (Didache 4:9-11). Barnabas 19:5-7 has the same lines.

Didache 4:10-11 speaks to masters before slaves: no harsh orders to slaves who share their hope, "or they may stop fearing the God who is over both of you," for God "does not come to call people by their standing." It does not question slavery itself.

In matters of food the Didache asks each to "carry what you can," but on one point it is strict: "be very careful to keep away from food sacrificed to idols, for it is the worship of dead gods" (Didache 6:3), as the apostles' letter asked of Gentiles (Acts 15:29).

The Didache gives the Lord's Prayer and says "Pray like this three times a day" (8:2-3), in the place of the Jewish morning, afternoon and evening prayers (Mishnah Berakhot 4:1). It also gives meal prayers (9:2-10:6), asks that no one come to prayer "with a bad conscience" (4:14), and lets prophets give thanks freely (10:7).

The Didache applies the Law of firstfruits to Gentile churches: the first of the winepress and threshing floor, cattle and sheep, bread, wine, oil, silver and clothing are given to the prophets, "for they are your high priests," or to the poor if there is no prophet (Didache 13:3-7), as Israel gave them to the priests (Numbers 18:12-13).

Didache 8:1-2 tells Christians not to fast or pray "like the hypocrites," who fast on Monday and Thursday. Kraft thinks the saying "originally may have referred to Pharisaic practices (cf. Matt. 23:13), although the Didachist might mean simply practicing Jews"; the words would also fit Christians who kept the same days. The word comes from Matthew 6 and 23. The church still fasts twice a week and prays three times a day, but on its own days and with its own prayer.

The Didache baptizes into the name of the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son (7:1, 3); says God calls "those whom the Spirit has made ready" (4:10); and speaks of prophets "speaking in the Spirit," whom it is the unforgivable sin to test or judge (11:7), while warning that not all who speak so are prophets (11:8).

sections.h: The threefold name in the Didache
sections.b: Didache 7:1 and 7:3 give the baptismal words "into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit," the form of Matthew 28:19. Kraft: the threefold formula is used "rather than the also popular baptism 'in the name of Jesus'," but this "does not, however, necessarily imply a conscious, full-blown 'trinitarian' theology as it was later defined." 9:5 also speaks of those "baptized into the Lord's name."

Eusebius (about AD 325) knew "the so-called Teachings of the Apostles" and put it among the "rejected writings," beside the Epistle of Barnabas (Church History 3.25.4, in McGiffert's translation; Kraft gives the Greek as notha, "illegitimate"), with no reason given. Athanasius in his Festal Letter 39 (AD 367) named "that which is called the Teaching of the Apostles" among books not in the canon but appointed by the Fathers to be read by those newly joining the church. It is in none of the canon lists cited on the Didache's page: the Catholic Catechism, the Westminster Confession, and the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church's list of the Holy Scriptures, which puts "The Didache" among books on church administration.

The Didache, or Teaching of the Twelve Apostles, is the church manual among the Apostolic Fathers: the Two Ways taught before baptism, rules for baptism, fasting and prayer, meal prayers over cup and bread, tests for traveling apostles and prophets, the Sunday gathering, overseers and deacons, and a warning about the last days. It was found in 1875 in the same manuscript that holds 1 and 2 Clement and Barnabas (Lake). Its Two Ways (Didache 1-6) is shared with Barnabas 18-20.
